text: Shirin Neshat (Persian: شیرین نشاط; born March 26, 1957) is an Iranian photographer and visual artist who lives in New York City and is known primarily for her work in film, video, and photography. Her artwork explores contrasts between Islam and the West, femininity and masculinity, public and private life, antiquity and modernity, and the intersections between these themes. Since the Islamic Revolution, she has stated that her art has focused on tyranny, dictatorship, oppression, and political injustice, noting that although she does not consider herself an activist, her art serves as an expression of protest and a cry for humanity. Neshat won the International Award at the XLVIII Venice Biennale in 1999 and the Silver Lion as best director at the 66th Venice Film Festival in 2009, and was named Artist of the Decade by HuffPost critic G. Roger Denson in 2010. She was a visiting critic in the photography department at the Yale School of Art in 2020. The fourth of five children of wealthy parents, she was raised in the religious city of Qazvin in north-western Iran in a "very warm, supportive Muslim family environment," where she learned traditional religious values from her maternal grandparents. Her father was a physician and her mother a homemaker; she recalled that both parents romanticized the West and gradually abandoned their values in favor of comfort, which served their class identity. Neshat attended a Catholic boarding school in Tehran, where her father encouraged his daughters to be individuals, take risks, learn, and see the world, and sent both daughters and sons to college. In 1975, she left Iran to study art at the University of California, Berkeley, completing her BA, MA, and MFA degrees, graduating in 1983. She moved to New York City, where she initially believed making art was not her profession. After meeting her future husband, who ran the Storefront for Art and Architecture in Manhattan, she spent ten years working with him, during which she made little art that she later destroyed, feeling intimidated by the New York art scene and dissatisfied with her work. In 1990, she returned to Iran, one year after Ayatollah Khomeini's death, describing it as one of the most shocking experiences of her life due to the dramatic shift in public behavior and physical appearance, which contrasted sharply with her memories of pre-revolution Iran. The Storefront's role as a cultural laboratory exposed her to artists, architects, and philosophers, reigniting her interest in art, and in 1993 she began creating seriously again, starting with photography. Her early works include the Unveiling (1993) and Women of Allah (1993–97) series, which examine femininity in the context of Islamic fundamentalism and militancy. The Women of Allah series features portraits of women overlaid with Persian calligraphy, reflecting on the social, cultural, and religious codes of Muslim societies and the complexities of oppositions such as man and woman. Neshat often presents two or more films simultaneously to create visual contrasts using motifs like light and dark, black and white, and male and female. She has also made narrative short films, such as Zarin. Her work addresses the social, political, and psychological dimensions of women's lives in contemporary Islamic societies, resisting stereotypical portrayals of Islam while recognizing the complex intellectual and religious forces shaping Muslim women's identities. Using Persian poetry and calligraphy, she explores themes such as martyrdom, exile, identity, and femininity. In 2001–02, she collaborated with singer Sussan Deyhim on Logic of the Birds, produced by RoseLee Goldberg, which premiered at the Lincoln Center Summer Festival in 2002 and toured to the Walker Art Institute in Minneapolis and Artangel in London. In an interview with Bomb magazine in 2000, she stated that music becomes the soul, the personal, and intuitive, neutralizing the sociopolitical aspects of the work and creating an emotionally evocative experience. In 2011, she created her second live performance, OverRuled, for Performa 11. When first using film, she was influenced by Iranian director Abbas Kiarostami. She directed several videos, including Anchorage (1996), Shadow under the Web (1997), Turbulent (1998), Rapture (1999), and Soliloquy (1999). In 1999, she won the International Award at the Venice Biennale with Turbulent and Rapture, a project involving nearly 250 extras produced by Galerie Jérôme de Noirmont, which achieved critical and public success after its worldwide avant-première at the Art Institute of Chicago in May 1999. With Rapture, she attempted to create pure photography to produce an aesthetic, poetic, and emotional impact. Games of Desire, a video and still-photography piece based in Laos, centers on elderly people singing folk songs with sexual lyrics, a practice nearing obsolescence, and was displayed at the Gladstone Gallery in Brussels from September 3 to October 3, then at Galerie Jérôme de Noirmont in Paris in November. In 2009, she won the Silver Lion for best director at the 66th Venice Film Festival for her directorial debut Women Without Men, based on Shahrnush Parsipur's novel, which examines the 1953 British-American-backed coup that replaced Iran's democratically elected government with a monarchy. She described the film as a "labour of love for six years" that speaks to the world and her country. In July 2009, she participated in a three-day hunger strike at the United Nations Headquarters in New York in protest of the 2009 Iranian presidential election. In 2010, she appeared in an episode of the German documentary television series Durch die Nacht mit ... with musician Henry Rollins. In 2022, she joined protests about the death of Mahsa Amini by showing her work Woman Life Freedom at Piccadilly Circus and Pendry West Hollywood. Her first solo exhibition was at Franklin Furnace in New York in 1993. A major retrospective organized by the Detroit Institute of Arts opened in 2013. In 2014, she had an exhibition titled "Afterwards" at the Mathaf: Arab Museum of Modern Art. In 2019, The Broad Museum in Los Angeles presented a 30-year retrospective, Shirin Neshat: I Will Greet the Sun Again, which traveled to the Modern Art Museum of Fort Worth in 2021. In 2022, she participated in the group exhibition "Eyes on Iran" at Franklin D. Roosevelt Four Freedoms State Park, Roosevelt Island, New York, in response to the Mahsa Amini protests. Shirin Neshat: I Will Greet the Sun Again at The Broad in Los Angeles (2019–2020) was her largest exhibition to date. In 2023, she presented The Fury at Fotografiska Stockholm, followed by a presentation at Fotografiska Berlin in 2024. Neshat was an artist in residence at the Wexner Center for the Arts in 2000 and at MASS MoCA in 2001. In 2004, she was awarded an honorary professorship at the Universität der Künste, Berlin. In 2006, she received The Dorothy and Lillian Gish Prize, one of the richest arts prizes, awarded annually to someone who has made an outstanding contribution to the beauty of the world and mankind's enjoyment and understanding of life. In 2015, she was selected and photographed by Annie Leibovitz for the 43rd Pirelli Calendar. At the 2017 Salzburg Festival, she directed Giuseppe Verdi's opera Aida, with Riccardo Muti as conductor and Anna Netrebko as the lead, and noted that sometimes the boundaries between Aida and herself are blurred.
